The dissertation develops hydrodynamic models expressed as conservation laws solved by finite volume discretization with high-order reconstruction and multi-stage time integration.
High-fidelity collisional-radiative models include detailed excitation and ionization kinetics and are benchmarked against shock tube experiments.
A mechanism reduction scheme based on level grouping reduces CR model complexity while maintaining accuracy for multidimensional flows.
Multifluid plasma models treat ions and electrons with separate conservation laws to capture deviations from hydrodynamic assumptions.
Excitation and deexcitation collision models in the multifluid framework obey the principle of detailed balance.
The multifluid CR model is applied to study ion acceleration in laser-plasma interactions, examining laser parameter effects.
The dissertation covers plasma physics applications in energy propulsion, space propulsion, plasma-assisted combustion, re-entry physics, and laser-plasma interactions.
Elementary processes modeled include collisional excitation/deexcitation, ionization/recombination, radiative transitions, and elastic collisions.
Numerical methods address stiff source terms, implicit time integration, and high-order spatial schemes for plasma simulations.
Benchmarking shows satisfactory agreement between CR model predictions and experimental electron density and temperature data.
The dissertation includes derivations of exchange source terms for multifluid CR kinetics starting from kinetic theory.
Laser-plasma interaction simulations incorporate electromagnetic wave propagation, collisional absorption, and ponderomotive forces.
The computational framework uses finite difference and transfer-matrix methods to solve electromagnetic wave equations.
Ion acceleration mechanisms are analyzed in detail with respect to laser parameters using the developed multifluid model.
The dissertation contains extensive validation against experimental data for argon, krypton, and xenon plasmas.
The work demonstrates that small deviations from hydrodynamic assumptions can be captured by multifluid models.
The CR mechanism reduction scheme is more accurate and efficient than standard level grouping approaches.
The multifluid excitation/deexcitation collision model ensures thermodynamic consistency via detailed balance.
The dissertation includes numerical benchmarks such as Euler equations, multi-fluid equations, and diffusion processes.
The hydrodynamic and multifluid models are suitable for multidimensional plasma flow calculations.
